passage: Sachin, it's Omkar here, and you would not believe the meeting yesterday. Forty minutes, five decisions, and not one person argued. I should have been happy, right? Instead my neck prickled. Kavita, who usually asks a hundred questions, asked none. Rahul just said "fine" to a budget I know worries him. So I stopped the meeting early and said, "From now on I will speak last, and tonight each of you send me one thing that could go wrong." Three emails were in my inbox before I got home. Sachin, quiet had not meant agreed, and I nearly missed it.

qa.q: How many decisions were made in forty minutes?
qa.a: Five decisions were made in forty minutes.

qa.q: Why did Omkar's neck prickle instead of feeling happy after the easy meeting?
qa.a: Omkar read the lack of argument as a warning sign; Kavita asking no questions and Rahul's quick "fine" suggested people were not speaking up, so unease replaced relief.

qa.q: What did Omkar change at the end of the meeting to invite honest views?
qa.a: Omkar decided to speak last and asked everyone to send one possible problem that evening, so people could say it in writing.

qa.q: Why might Kavita, who usually asks many questions, have stayed silent?
qa.a: Kavita may have felt the mood made questions unwelcome, or may have assumed others agreed; the silence could hide a concern.

grounding: Someone running a meeting notices that discussions end too easily and reads the silence as a warning that people are not speaking up.

passage: I sit two seats from Kiran, so I saw what happened after Tuesday's planning call. Six of us said "fine" to the new schedule in under a minute. Kiran, our manager, did not smile. Kiran looked around the table, tapped a pen twice, and said, "That was too easy. Nikhil, tell me what would break this plan." Nikhil laughed, went red, then said the testing time was too short. Then Meera said the same thing, and then me. I cannot say what Kiran felt at that point; Kiran just wrote things down and said, "Thank you, that is more useful than a yes."

qa.q: How many people said "fine" to the new schedule?
qa.a: Six people said "fine" to the new schedule in under a minute.

qa.q: What might Kiran have been thinking when saying "That was too easy"?
qa.a: Kiran seems to have sensed that quick agreement meant people were holding back, and felt concerned rather than relieved; the narrator cannot be sure of Kiran's exact feeling.

qa.q: What choice by Kiran got real concerns onto the table?
qa.a: Kiran named the easy agreement, asked one person directly what would break the plan, and thanked those who then spoke up.

qa.q: What might Nikhil have been feeling when laughing, going red and then answering?
qa.a: Nikhil probably felt caught off guard and a little embarrassed, but also relieved to have permission to say the testing time was too short.

grounding: A manager senses false harmony when a discussion ends too easily and reads it as people not speaking up, seen by a team member.
